body:
Not a bad solution to people just blindly using the query APIs and expecting the best performance I suppose... I do wonder if this is absolutely necessary though. It's not really *misuse* or incorrect usage of the API, it's just suboptimal.

There is not (in most cases) going to be a significant difference in performance between caching the query objects (or new result objects should #113970 be merged) and allocating them once per-frame for people who are only doing a handful of queries per-frame (which I would imagine is most users' situation, especially considering that the current API's performance doesn't allow for a large amount of queries in the first place).

I've personally tested this in a few of my own query-heavy projects on a small variety of (mostly low to mid-range desktop/laptop) hardware, and caching parameter objects didn't result in a noticeable difference in performance until you start doing a quite large amount of (several hundred plus) queries per frame.

Maybe on very low-end or mobile hardware it does become a significant issue faster? If so I think this is probably a reasonable way to inform newer or more inexperienced users of the optimal usage pattern, but I think it should absolutely be able to be ignored/disabled at the project settings level, and I would still argue that the responsibility of informing users of the optimal usage of an API should belong to documentation and not editor warnings (also, it should be obvious that allocating something every frame is going to be slower than allocating something once).

Documentation is free at both runtime and compile time, and I'm very wary in particular of the template bloat required for this, considering what we gain from doing it, just for people who are not willing to read documentation when they're seeing performance that doesn't meet their expectations. Granted, I can't really see a better way to go about implementing this warning if it is deemed to be necessary, the current approach is likely as good as it gets.

Actually, it seems that the docs don't even suggest doing this in the optimal way currently, so it would be very strange to warn about the exact usage encouraged by the docs https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/physics/ray-casting.html#raycast-query

I think the docs need to be updated to suggest the optimal usage for sure, but my preference would be to leave the current examples as-is for simplicity (the parameter objects' `create()` APIs would become essentially useless if we enforce this, save for one-off queries in non-process methods), and to add a section encouraging reuse of parameter objects when users need more performance or want to be conscious of memory churn, rather than only showing the most optimal usage in every example and throwing warnings when it's done differently (especially considering most users aren't going to see significant performance improvements anyway).

I can open a PR tomorrow to update the relevant areas in the docs regarding reuse of query parameter objects, and when #113970 is merged I'd be happy to make a follow-up PR to do the same for the new result objects, if that's okay. If another approach is preferred, happy to hear suggestions.

I would argue all the docs and demos should be updated yes, reusing objects when they are used (directly or indirectly) over multiple ticks in `_physics_process`. There are still use cases for creating temporary variables and/or using `create`, for example in response to a timer reaching zero after a countdown, or other one-offs. But once you start querying 60 times per second (with the default tick rate) you probably shouldn't be redoing the allocation, even if it isn't a performance issue.

I do agree it can be a non-issue for performance in practice in many cases (especially in small games), but I think warnings can be opinionated and encourage good practice. I guess it should be possible to disable them though.

Let's see what others think.

> As an alternative, I first considered trying to use the GDScript analyzer to see where the instance is created (I wanted to check if it is assigned to a class member), but this is complicated since it would also be valid to put it in a container (like an array or a dictionary), and good luck detecting that case. 

Can you do the opposite, and just detect when it is created as a local var? Bear in mind this kind of thing doesn't need to detect all cases, just common cases that could be improved (with a tooltip in the IDE or something).

> I've personally tested this in a few of my own query-heavy projects on a small variety of (mostly low to mid-range desktop/laptop) hardware, and caching parameter objects didn't result in a noticeable difference in performance until you start doing a quite large amount of (several hundred plus) queries per frame.

What language did you try?

I'm not a c# guy, but seeing https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7842 , that is suggestive this kind of thing may be more of a problem in c#, if it e.g. triggers garbage collection.

As an aside I agree that it's worth being exhaustive seeing what is achievable with the GDScriptAnalyzer (although admittedly that won't help for c#, and this kind of approach would work for all languages).

> What language did you try?

GDScript and C++ (GDExtension). I'm not a fan of garbage collected languages so I avoid them when I can now (and C# has never actually given me improvements over GDScript performance-wise except in heavy cases where I'm just more comfortable switching to C++ anyway). I should have considered C# in this equation though you're right.

> I do agree it can be a non-issue for performance in practice in many cases (especially in small games), but I think warnings can be opinionated and encourage good practice.

That's a fair point, and I do agree there isn't a real reason beyond laziness / shorter code for quick prototyping to be doing it the way suggested in the docs currently. I'm on board with the warning as long as it's able to be ignored somehow.

I'm trying to imagine a real-world case where this could happen, but it is theoretically possible for "one-off" code that allocates the query params inline to trigger this warning if said one-off code is ever called programmatically (like for instance a chest spewing out items once per frame in a stream, not that that would require a ray cast, but to illustrate the point).

In most situations I can think of with that problem though, I can't imagine a reason why you wouldn't still be able to just create the object once and reuse it, so maybe this is more something to consider regarding the wording of the warning and not an issue with the warning itself (I don't think it should mention physics ticks in the warning message if we can confirm this is possible, and honestly even if it isn't, since you're allowed to perform these queries in idle process as well).

> I would argue all the docs and demos should be updated yes, reusing objects when they are used (directly or indirectly) over multiple ticks in _physics_process.

Just to confirm, would it likely be best to update each of the doc examples which are querying over multiple ticks to do something like this instead? Also, would the comment above the param object declaration be helpful, perhaps even if only on the first such example of reuse on the page?

```gdscript
@onready var space_state := get_world_2d().direct_space_state

# Reuse parameter object instead of reallocating every physics tick.
var query := PhysicsRayQueryParameters2D.new()

func _physics_process(delta):
    # Use global coordinates, not local to node.
    query.from = Vector2(0, 0)
    query.to = Vector2(50, 100)
    var result = space_state.intersect_ray(query)
```

I haven't contributed to docs before specifically yet, I can try to whip this up as a draft shortly though, since it seems to be a good idea regardless of whether this or the new query API gets merged.

Just bringing up again, I think the error message shouldn't mention "physics ticks" and `_physics_process()` directly, since there are legitimate reasons to be performing queries in e.g. `_process()` and the error would then point to an unrelated method which would be confusing.

EDIT: The new wording is definitely better with "methods such as", thanks!

I want to be clear I'm not saying all of this code is bad. Probably many of the code samples are based on examples from the documentation, and probably in all cases performance was not noticeably affected. At least the results show that sub-optimal use does occur in the real world.

Given that there are small projects where the frequent allocations don't matter, I would like to add a way to disable the warning. @lawnjelly wrote on RocketChat:

> I would, and make sure it doesn't spam. Also use `GLOBAL_GET_CACHED` and don't call it every tick, just delay the timer so it only refreshes every so many times.

I'm not sure how this should be implemented exactly (feel free to push to this branch @lawnjelly if you want).

Edit: I added the project setting.
I'll tentatively say this is more appropriate for 4.9, but the warning seems appropriate given we have systems mitigating this exact problem

Just to at least have said my peace, I think this warning is somewhat overzealous to have enabled by default, and will likely annoy people.

I am admittedly not interacting much with actual game projects when it comes to writing physics code these days, but I suspect this will become one of those settings that I find myself disabling in almost every project, but I am perhaps more painfully aware of what/where I'm allocating compared to more casual GDScript users.

Also, not that we really have the mechanisms for this, but I feel like this needs some kind of ability to suppress on a case-by-case basis as well. Having it be all-or-nothing seems problematic for large-scale codebases.

I would also say that something like this really should show the source of the warning, especially given how much existing code it's going to complain about. The editor will probably do a decent job of showing the source for GDScript specifically, and any log files will show the script backtraces, but C# might be a different story (I haven't tested) and GDExtension code will presumably be completely in the dark.

EDIT: Oh, and mention the setting in the warning as well.
I don't want these warnings in the navigation objects.
